newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico stocks slide at close on U.S. Senate vote.
newsitem.headline: Mexico stocks slide at close on U.S. Senate vote.

text.p: Mexican stocks fell sharply Thursday following news the U.S. Senate acted to rebuke Mexico as an ally in the war on drugs.

"This (resolution) hit the bourse, because although it was not outright decertification, it still makes dealers nervous. We started to slide faster once the news broke as they used it as a pretext to step up profit-taking" a floor trader said.
The leading IPC share index ended down 57.30 points, or 1.48 percent, at 3,809.90.
Key U.S. senators drafted a resolution that stopped short of proposing decertification, but would still criticise Mexico's drug-fighting efforts.
Traders remarked on the sharp drop posted by telecommunications firm Telmex in both New York and Mexico, but offered different interpretations.
Telmex L shares plunged 78 centavos (10 cents) to 15.80 pesos ($1.99), while its ADRs ended off two dollars at 39-5/8.
"The market was weighed down again by Telmex. It broke through the 41-mark on Wall Street yesterday, met with resistance and that's where sellers stepped in," the floor trader added.
Telmex L class accounted for almost one-quarter of all shares traded in regular dealing.
ADRs listed by construction firm ICA fell 1/4 to 16-1/8 while conglomerate Desc actually gained 1/4 to 26-3/4.
The trading volume scoreboard chalked up an unheard-of 1.07 billion shares traded, or some 10 times that posted during an average session.

Dealers noted that four last-minute cross trades accounted for 981.4 million of nominal total volume. The trades were in A and B class shares listed by cable manufacturer Latinca, as part of a deal whereby Condumex, part of the Carso group, acquired the company.
Carso shares bucked the general downward trend to gain 15 centavos (two cents) to 46.05 pesos ($5.81).
On the broad market, meanwhile, 107 stocks changed hands, of which decliners outnumbered gainers by 45 to 27.
Latincasa A and B shares topped the gainers' list, which both climbed 20 centavos (less than three cents) to 50 centavos (six cents).
Dealers noted financial groups were among the prominent sliders on a combination of profit-taking and fears of a forthcoming hike in U.S. interest rates.
Mexican financial markets close on Friday, March 21, to honour of Benito Juarez, a 19th-century president and national hero.
